summary:
A value that fills **more than half** the list survives any cancelling: pair each copy of it with a
different value and there are copies left over. Boyer–Moore voting does exactly that in one pass with
two variables, O(n) time and O(1) space.

question.md:
One value appears in more than half of the readings. Return it.

- **More than half** means strictly more than n/2: in 7 readings it appears at least 4 times; in 8,
  at least 5. It's guaranteed to exist, so there's no "no answer" case to handle.
- **Values can be negative** and as large as ±10⁹, so you can't index an array by value.
- **Size:** up to 10⁵ readings.
- The guarantee is what makes the clever O(1)-space method valid. Without it, you'd need a second
  pass to confirm the candidate.

think.md:
Take `[2, 8, 8, 1, 8, 8, 3, 8, 2]`: 8 appears 5 times out of 9.

Counting with a hash map clearly works. But here's a sharper observation: **pair up readings that
are different and throw both away.** Each 8 can be paired with at most one non-8, and there are only
4 non-8s. However you pair things, at least one 8 survives, and nothing else can survive more than 8
does.

think.caption: Four non-8s can cancel at most four 8s. The fifth 8 survives.

think.md:
Boyer–Moore turns that into a scan: keep a **candidate** and a **count**. A matching reading adds a
vote; a different reading cancels one; when the count hits zero, the next reading becomes the new
candidate. Whatever is left at the end is the majority.

Another view, useful for the sorting approach: a value covering more than half the positions of a
**sorted** list must cover the middle position.

approaches.title: Count every value by scanning

idea.md: For each reading, count its copies with a full scan. The first one whose count exceeds n/2 is the answer.

build: For each reading `r`, count how many readings equal `r`.

lines.text: Try each reading as the answer.
Count its copies. More than half (`c × 2 > n`, which avoids rounding issues with `n / 2`) means it's the majority.

complexity.md: **Time O(n²):** each candidate costs a full scan. **Space O(1).**

walk.title: Count each reading's copies with a full scan until one has more than half.

limits.md: The same values get recounted over and over. Count each value once, or use the order a sort provides.

idea.md: In sorted order the majority's copies form one block longer than n/2. Any block that long must cover index `n // 2`, so the answer is simply `sorted[n // 2]`.

lines.text: Sorted copy: each value's copies form one contiguous block.
A block longer than half the list can't fit entirely left or right of the middle, so it covers index n / 2.

notes.c: Read the answer before freeing the copy.

complexity.md: **Time O(n log n).** **Space O(n)** for the copy.

steps.text: A value filling more than half the slots must cover index n // 2 = 4.

walk.title: Sort; the majority value always covers the middle position.

limits.md: Sorting orders all values when we only need the one that dominates. Counting avoids the log factor.

approaches.title: Count with a hash map

idea.md: Count readings in a hash map as you go. As soon as some count exceeds n/2, return that value.

build: Create an empty value → count map.
For each reading, add 1 to its count; if `count × 2 > n`, return it.

lines.text: C has no hash map: a slot holds a value, its count and an in-use flag, and `slotOf` scrambles a value into a starting slot.
Counts per value, filled as we go.

notes.c: A power-of-two table at least 2n big, zeroed by `calloc`.

lines.text: Add one to this reading's count.

notes.c: Probe from the value's slot to its entry (or an empty slot) and claim it.

lines.text: The first count to pass half is the majority; stop right there.

notes.cpp: `++count[r]` creates the entry at 0 if needed, increments it, and gives the new value.

notes.c: Free the table and return the answer found.

complexity.md: **Time O(n)** on average. **Space O(n)**: up to about n/2 distinct values can be stored.

walk.title: Count every value in a hash map; stop when a count passes n / 2.

limits.md: The map remembers every distinct value even though only one of them matters. Voting needs just one candidate and one counter.

approaches.title: Boyer–Moore voting

idea.md:
Keep `candidate` and `count`, starting at count 0. For each reading:

- count 0 → this reading becomes the candidate with count 1;
- same as the candidate → count + 1;
- different → count − 1 (it cancels one vote).

**Why it works:** every decrement pairs one candidate copy with one different reading and
discards both. Discarding two *different* values from a list keeps the majority a majority of
what remains (it loses at most one of its copies, while the list shrinks by two). At the end,
what's left uncancelled can only be the majority.

build: For each reading: if `count == 0`, set `candidate` to it.
Then `count += 1` if it equals the candidate, else `count −= 1`.

lines.text: No candidate yet: a count of 0 means "the next reading takes over".
All earlier readings have cancelled each other out, so start fresh with this one.
A match strengthens the candidate; a different value cancels one of its votes (both are discarded as a pair).
With a guaranteed majority, the survivor is it. (Without the guarantee you'd recount the candidate in a second pass to confirm.)

complexity.md: **Time O(n):** one pass. **Space O(1):** two variables.

steps.text: Reading 2: count is 0, so 2 becomes the candidate (count 1).
Reading 8: 8 differs: it cancels one vote, count 0.
Reading 8: count is 0, so 8 becomes the candidate (count 1).
Reading 1: 1 differs: it cancels one vote, count 0.
Reading 8: count is 0, so 8 becomes the candidate (count 1).
Reading 3: 3 differs: it cancels one vote, count 1.
Reading 2: 2 differs: it cancels one vote, count 1.

walk.title: Boyer–Moore voting: different values cancel in pairs; the majority can't be cancelled out.

takeaways.md:
- A strict majority can't be cancelled out: pairing it against everything else leaves copies over.
  That's **Boyer–Moore voting**, O(1) space.
- The guarantee matters. If a majority might not exist, verify the candidate with a second count.
- The sorting trick (majority covers the middle index) is a handy one-liner when O(n log n) is fine.
- The idea generalises: at most two values can exceed n/3 (see **Strong Candidates**), with two
  candidate slots.
